introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, duration one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: read the instructions carefully before you start; use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the question booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0755 Geology - 1'; fill in the information required in the spaces above (candidate number and name; centre number and name) and on the answer sheet. Answer ALL the 50 questions. All questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. If you change your mind, erase the first mark carefully, then mark your new answer. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet, using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet; do not attempt to leave the examination hall with it. Reference 00/0755/1.

questions.enonce_markdown: An interstellar cloud of dust, hydrogen, helium and other ionized gases is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **nebula** is an interstellar cloud of dust and gas (mainly hydrogen and helium, partly ionized). Nebulae are the birthplaces of stars and planetary systems: the solar nebula collapsed to form the Sun and the planets. A comet is a small icy body of the solar system, a galaxy is a huge assembly of stars, gas and dust, and a meteor is the streak of light produced when a meteoroid burns up in the atmosphere.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The closest galaxy to the planet Earth is:

*Options as printed:* A) Milky Way galaxy   B) Andromeda galaxy   C) Elliptical galaxy   D) Irregular galaxy
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Earth and the whole solar system lie **inside the Milky Way galaxy**, so the Milky Way is the galaxy that is closest to the Earth (it is the one that contains it). 'Elliptical' and 'irregular' are shapes (types) of galaxies, not names of a particular galaxy. Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy beyond our own (about 2.5 million light-years away), so it is the right answer only if the question means 'the closest other large galaxy'.

**Intended answer: A (Milky Way galaxy).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: What name is given to the layer of the Earth between 35km and 2900km?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho) lies at an average depth of about 35 km under the continents and marks the base of the crust. The Gutenberg discontinuity lies at about 2900 km and marks the top of the outer core. The whole layer between these two boundaries is the **mantle**. The 'upper mantle' and 'lower mantle' are only parts of it (the boundary between them is at about 660-700 km), and the outer core begins at 2900 km.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 1 below is the graph showing the velocity-depth curves of earthquake waves X and Y. Study the graph and answer questions 4 and 5.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: velocity-depth curves of earthquake waves X and Y (velocity in km/s on the vertical axis, ticks 4 to 14; depth in km on the horizontal axis, ticks 0, 2000, 4000, 6000). Curve Y starts at about 8 km/s at the surface, rises to about 14-15 km/s, drops abruptly at about 2900 km and then rises again; curve X starts near 4 km/s, rises to about 7 km/s and stops at the same depth as the drop of Y.*

(Figure 1 is used for questions 4 and 5.)

Determine the average velocity of wave Y at the surface of the Earth:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Read the curve of wave Y at depth 0 km (where it leaves the vertical axis): it starts at the level of the **8 km/s** tick. Wave Y is the primary (P) wave, which travels faster than the shear wave X and, in the crust and uppermost mantle, has a velocity of about 6-8 km/s. It rises to about 14 km/s at the base of the mantle, then falls sharply on entering the liquid outer core. The values 12 and 14 km/s are reached only deep in the Earth and 0 km/s is the velocity of an S wave in a liquid, not of Y at the surface.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 1 below is the graph showing the velocity-depth curves of earthquake waves X and Y. Study the graph and answer questions 4 and 5.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: velocity-depth curves of earthquake waves X and Y (velocity in km/s on the vertical axis, ticks 4 to 14; depth in km on the horizontal axis, ticks 0, 2000, 4000, 6000). Curve Y starts at about 8 km/s at the surface, rises to about 14-15 km/s, drops abruptly at about 2900 km and then rises again; curve X starts near 4 km/s, rises to about 7 km/s and stops at the same depth as the drop of Y.*

(Figure 1 is used for questions 4 and 5.)

The deepest depth attained by wave X is approximately:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Curve X is the S (shear) wave. It stops at the same depth as the sudden fall of the P wave Y, that is at the core-mantle (Gutenberg) boundary, at about **2900 km**. S waves cannot cross the outer core because shear waves do not travel through a liquid. This is the evidence that the outer core is liquid. The graph is read approximately (the end of the X curve lies just under 3000 km on the printed scale), and only 2900 km is a recognised boundary of the Earth.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Seismic waves that cause the components of a rock to vibrate perpendicularly to the direction of wave propagation are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In **shear waves (S waves)** the particles of the rock oscillate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels (transverse motion). In compressional waves (P waves) the particles move back and forth in the direction of propagation. Love and Rayleigh waves are surface waves (Love waves move the ground horizontally and Rayleigh waves in a rolling, elliptical motion), they are not the body waves described by the wording 'components of a rock'.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal drawing below (Figure 2) and answer questions 7 and 8.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: crystal drawing, a six-sided (hexagonal) prism with a horizontal axis +a1 drawn towards the left.*

(Figure 2 is used for questions 7 and 8.)

How many diagonal planes of symmetry does this crystal have?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The crystal is a hexagonal prism (normal class 6/m 2/m 2/m). It has 7 planes of symmetry in all: 1 horizontal (equatorial) plane and 6 vertical planes. The 6 vertical planes are of two kinds: **3 axial planes** (each contains one of the crystallographic a axes and the c axis) and **3 diagonal planes** (each bisects the angle between two a axes, passing through opposite edges or faces of the prism). So the crystal has 3 diagonal planes. The number 7 is the total of all planes of symmetry, not only the diagonal ones.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal drawing below (Figure 2) and answer questions 7 and 8.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: crystal drawing, a six-sided (hexagonal) prism with a horizontal axis +a1 drawn towards the left.*

(Figure 2 is used for questions 7 and 8.)

An example of a mineral with such a habit is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The drawing shows a six-sided prism, the habit of the hexagonal system. **Apatite**, $\mathrm{Ca_5(PO_4)_3(F,Cl,OH)}$, crystallises in the hexagonal system as hexagonal prisms. Rutile, idocrase (vesuvianite) and zircon all crystallise in the tetragonal system and form four-sided prisms.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A crystal face has as parameters 2a, b, 1c. What is the Miller Index of this face?

*Options as printed:* A) 201   B) 402   C) 102   D) 202
questions.corrige_markdown:
Miller indices are found in three steps: (1) write the intercepts on the a, b and c axes; (2) take the reciprocals; (3) clear the fractions. The printed parameters '2a, b, 1c' read literally give intercepts $2, 1, 1$, hence reciprocals $\tfrac12, 1, 1$ and, after multiplying by 2, the index $(122)$, which is **not among the four options**. The options show that the face was probably meant to be parallel to the b axis (parameters $2a, \infty b, 1c$, the infinity symbol being lost in the print): the intercepts are then $2, \infty, 1$, the reciprocals $\tfrac12, 0, 1$ and the index $(102)$, option C. Because the printed parameters and the options do not agree, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: C (102).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which physical property of a given mineral displays the greatest variation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Colour** is the least reliable property for identifying a mineral, because traces of impurities (for example in quartz, which can be colourless, pink, purple or smoky) and weathering change it from one specimen to another. Hardness (Mohs scale), lustre and streak (colour of the powder) are much more constant for a given mineral.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study (Figure 3) below which shows a section of a silicate mineral showing cleavage planes and use it to answer questions 11 and 12.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: section of a silicate mineral showing two sets of cleavage planes (forming a lattice of rhombs) and the faces labelled 1-10 (one bar over the 1 of the second index) and 110.*

(Figure 3 is used for questions 11 and 12.)

Identify the silicate mineral:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The figure shows two sets of cleavage planes intersecting at about **56 degrees and 124 degrees** (a lattice of flattened rhombs). This pair of cleavages, parallel to the {110} faces, is the diagnostic feature of the **amphiboles**, of which hornblende is the common example. Pyroxene also has two cleavages but they meet at nearly 90 degrees (87 and 93 degrees). Biotite has a single perfect cleavage (sheets) and olivine has no good cleavage.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study (Figure 3) below which shows a section of a silicate mineral showing cleavage planes and use it to answer questions 11 and 12.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: section of a silicate mineral showing two sets of cleavage planes (forming a lattice of rhombs) and the faces labelled 1-10 (one bar over the 1 of the second index) and 110.*

(Figure 3 is used for questions 11 and 12.)

The silicate mineral in question 11 above has a:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hornblende (an amphibole) is an inosilicate with **double chains** of silica tetrahedra (two single chains linked by shared oxygens, unit $\mathrm{Si_4O_{11}}$). This double chain explains the 56 and 124 degree cleavage. Pyroxenes have single chains, micas such as biotite have sheets (phyllosilicates) and olivine has isolated tetrahedra (nesosilicate).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is an incomplete presentation of the Bowen's Reaction Series (Figure 4). Use it to answer questions 13 and 14.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: incomplete Bowen's Reaction Series. Discontinuous series (left): olivine, orthorombic pyroxene, monoclinic pyroxene, X, biotite; continuous series (right, arrows downwards): anorthite, bytownite, labradorite, andesine, oligoclase, albite; the two series meet at potash feldspar, muscovite, quartz.*

(Figure 4 is used for questions 13 and 14.)

Identify the mineral represented by the letter X.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The discontinuous branch of Bowen's series runs, with falling temperature: olivine, orthopyroxene (orthorhombic, hypersthene or enstatite), clinopyroxene (monoclinic, augite), **amphibole (hornblende)** and then biotite. The letter X lies between monoclinic pyroxene and biotite, so it is hornblende. Augite is the monoclinic pyroxene already shown, hypersthene is the orthorhombic pyroxene already shown, and no pyroxene is triclinic in this series.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is an incomplete presentation of the Bowen's Reaction Series (Figure 4). Use it to answer questions 13 and 14.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: incomplete Bowen's Reaction Series. Discontinuous series (left): olivine, orthorombic pyroxene, monoclinic pyroxene, X, biotite; continuous series (right, arrows downwards): anorthite, bytownite, labradorite, andesine, oligoclase, albite; the two series meet at potash feldspar, muscovite, quartz.*

(Figure 4 is used for questions 13 and 14.)

An example of a mineral in the continuous series which is an essential mineral in gabbro is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The continuous series is the plagioclase feldspar series, from calcium-rich (anorthite) to sodium-rich (albite). **Gabbro** is a basic rock made of calcium-rich plagioclase (labradorite, about An50-70) and pyroxene (augite), sometimes with olivine. Oligoclase and andesine are sodium-richer plagioclases found in intermediate to acid rocks (diorite, granodiorite) and anorthite is almost pure calcium feldspar, characteristic of anorthosite and not the usual plagioclase of gabbro.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which of the following layers is basaltic magma most likely to originate?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Basaltic magma is produced by **partial melting of peridotite in the upper mantle**, for example by decompression melting beneath mid-ocean ridges and hot spots. Melting of the lower or upper continental crust gives more silica-rich (granitic or andesitic) magmas, and the lower mantle is too deep and is not the source of the basalts that reach the surface.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An igneous rock X was analysed as having the following composition $\mathrm{SiO_2}=48.5\%$, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}=3.2\%$, $\mathrm{CaO}=11.7\%$, $\mathrm{FeO}=8.5\%$, Others$=28.1\%$. Use this information to answer questions 16 and 17.

If this rock is phaneritic, it is most likely to be:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The silica content is 48.5 %, which places the rock in the **basic** group (about 45-52 % $\mathrm{SiO_2}$), with high CaO and iron oxides (the percentages add up to 100 %: $48.5+3.2+11.7+8.5+28.1=100.0$). A basic rock with a phaneritic (coarse-grained, plutonic) texture is **gabbro** (the fine-grained equivalent is basalt). Granite (acid, about 70 % silica) and diorite (intermediate, 52-63 %) have more silica, and peridotite is ultrabasic (below 45 % silica).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An igneous rock X was analysed as having the following composition $\mathrm{SiO_2}=48.5\%$, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}=3.2\%$, $\mathrm{CaO}=11.7\%$, $\mathrm{FeO}=8.5\%$, Others$=28.1\%$. Use this information to answer questions 16 and 17.

The essential minerals of the rock mentioned in 16 above will be:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rock is gabbro, whose essential minerals are calcium-rich plagioclase (**labradorite**) and pyroxene (**augite**). Quartz and micas belong to acid rocks (granite), andesine and hornblende to diorite, so options A, B and D describe acid or intermediate rocks.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 below shows the texture of an igneous rock. Study it and answer questions 18 and 19.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: texture of an igneous rock (large angular crystals set in a fine-grained matrix with scattered small grains; scale bar 5 mm).*

(Figure 5 is used for questions 18 and 19.)

Identify the texture shown on the diagram above:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The drawing shows a few large, well-formed crystals (**phenocrysts**) set in a much finer-grained groundmass: this is the **porphyritic** texture. Graphic texture is an intergrowth of quartz in feldspar that looks like cuneiform writing, ophitic texture has laths of plagioclase enclosed in larger pyroxene crystals and poikilitic texture has small crystals enclosed in a large crystal.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 below shows the texture of an igneous rock. Study it and answer questions 18 and 19.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: texture of an igneous rock (large angular crystals set in a fine-grained matrix with scattered small grains; scale bar 5 mm).*

(Figure 5 is used for questions 18 and 19.)

The texture mentioned in question 18 was most likely formed as a result of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A porphyritic texture records **two stages of cooling**: the large phenocrysts grew slowly at depth, then the magma rose and the remaining melt cooled quickly to a fine groundmass (or the magma crystallised under conditions where nucleation and growth rates differed). It is therefore the result of crystallisation in an environment where crystals grow at different rates. Simultaneous crystallisation gives an even-grained rock, and uniformly very slow cooling gives a coarse, equigranular rock.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Crystallisation in the plutonic and volcanic environments
Crystallization in an environment where crystals grow at different rates

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the marble produced from the recrystallization reaction below:

$2\,\mathrm{CaCO_3.MgCO_3} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CaCO_3} + \mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4} + 2\,\mathrm{CO_2}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The reaction is the metamorphism of an impure dolomitic limestone: dolomite plus silica gives calcite, a magnesium silicate and carbon dioxide. The atoms balance (left: Ca 2, Mg 2, C 4, Si 1, O 14; right: the same). The silicate formed is $\mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4}$, which is **forsterite** (the magnesium end-member of olivine), so the rock is a forsterite marble. Diopside is $\mathrm{CaMgSi_2O_6}$, wollastonite $\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$ and tremolite is a calcium-magnesium amphibole containing OH.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following metarmorphic facies is in order from the lowest to the highest grade.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In order of increasing temperature and depth the facies are: zeolite, (prehnite-pumpellyite), greenschist, amphibolite and granulite. Blueschist is a high-pressure, low-temperature facies of subduction zones and is placed after zeolite and before greenschist in the printed list. Option A is the only one that starts with zeolite (the lowest grade) and ends with amphibolite (the highest) with greenschist before amphibolite. Option B starts with blueschist, option C puts greenschist before blueschist and option D lists the highest grades first, ending with the lowest.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Zeolite, blue schist, green schist, amphibolite;
Blue schist, zeolite, green schist, amphibolite;
Zeolite, green schist, blue schist, amphibolite;
Green schist, amphibolite, blue schist, zeolite.

questions.enonce_markdown: The occurrence of porphyroblasts in a metamorphic rock indicates:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Porphyroblasts** are large crystals (for example garnet, staurolite or andalusite) that grew during metamorphism in a finer-grained matrix: the rock shows coarse grains surrounded by finer grains. The preferred orientation of minerals is foliation, not porphyroblasts, and 'formation in two different environments' describes a porphyritic igneous rock or a rock with two metamorphic events, not what porphyroblasts show by themselves.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Preferred orientation of minerals due to stress
Coarse grains surrounded by finer grains
Ability of minerals to move within metamorphic environment

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 6) shows a folded strata affected by a fault. Study and answer questions 23, 24 and 25.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: block diagram of folded strata affected by a fault (the fault F cuts across the fold, an arrow on the right shows the downthrown side; the outcrop pattern closes towards the right of the block and the front face shows a U-shaped (bowl-like) fold).*

(Figure 6 is used for questions 23, 24 and 25.)

Identify the type of fold shown on the diagram:
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the front face of the block the beds curve downwards and come back up, a trough (U-shape, limbs dipping towards the axis): the fold is a **synform**. The word 'syncline' also requires that the youngest beds lie in the core of the fold, and the diagram gives no ages for the layers, so the neutral name 'synform' (shape only) is the correct one. An antiform or anticline would show an arch with the limbs dipping away from the axis.

After a dip-slip fault the downthrown block is eroded to the same level as the upthrown block, so it exposes the higher (younger) part of the structure. For a synform (a trough) the higher part is the wider part, so the outcrop of the fold is **wider on the downthrown side**; for an antiform it would be narrower. The printed options are badly worded (the same phrase 'on the downthrown side' appears in options A to C, and option D describes a change along the fold instead of a comparison) and the position of the fault in the drawing is hard to read, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the information below to answer questions 26 and 27. A sediment sample from a certain basin was analysed and found to have quartz, feldspar, biotite and muscovite in various proportions.

If this sediment sample is described as sub-mature, it is due to the relative abundance of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Mineralogical maturity increases as the unstable minerals are destroyed by weathering and transport, until only quartz remains (a mature sediment is a quartz arenite). A sample that is only **sub-mature** still contains a significant proportion of **feldspar**, which is quite unstable in weathering (it alters to clay), together with micas. Quartz abundance would make the sample more mature, not less. Micas (biotite and muscovite) are also less stable than quartz but feldspar is the usual indicator used in the classification (arkose, subarkose).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the information below to answer questions 26 and 27. A sediment sample from a certain basin was analysed and found to have quartz, feldspar, biotite and muscovite in various proportions.

The shape of most of the quartz grains in the sample can be described as:

*Options as printed:* A) Euhedral   B) Sub rounded   C) Sub-angular   D) Rounded
questions.corrige_markdown:
Euhedral is a term for crystals bounded by their own faces (igneous or authigenic), not for transported sedimentary grains, so A is out. A sub-mature sediment has travelled a moderate distance, so its quartz grains are expected to be moderately rounded: **sub-rounded**. The printed question gives no grain data (no figure, no sieve analysis or transport history), so this is an expectation rather than a deduction and sub-angular is also defendable; the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Sub rounded).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The sand commonly used in the building industry in Cameroon today is obtained from:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Building sand in Cameroon is dredged or dug mainly from **river (stream) channels** and river beds (for example the Wouri, Sanaga and their tributaries): river sand is clean, angular to sub-angular and well sorted, with little salt. Options A, B and D all refer to the coast; beach and littoral sand contains salt and shell fragments, which corrode reinforcement and weaken concrete, and extraction from beaches is discouraged because of coastal erosion.

**Answer: C.**

Figure 7 below is a profile commonly attained by many streams. Use it to answer questions 29 and 30.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: stream profile (height in m against distance) with a break of slope, the knick point, between an upper gentle concave profile and a lower steeper profile.*

(Figure 7 is used for questions 29 and 30.)

What phenomenon does the knick point in the diagram represent?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A knick point is a break of slope in the long profile of a river that marks the place where a new cycle of erosion, started by a **fall of base level** (uplift of the land or fall in sea level), is working its way upstream. This renewal of erosion is called **rejuvenation**. Isostatic adjustment and balance are movements of the crust and not a feature of the river profile, and backward (headward) erosion describes the lengthening of the valley, not the break of slope.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 7 below is a profile commonly attained by many streams. Use it to answer questions 29 and 30.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: stream profile (height in m against distance) with a break of slope, the knick point, between an upper gentle concave profile and a lower steeper profile.*

(Figure 7 is used for questions 29 and 30.)

How many baselines can be seen on this profile?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The profile is made of two graded sections: the upper, gentle section, which is graded to the **old base level** (it ends at the knick point where the profile flattens), and the lower, steeper section produced after the fall of base level, which is graded to the **new (present) base level** at the end of the profile. There are therefore **2 base levels**. The reading follows the drawing, where the curve is flat above the knick point and reaches the horizontal axis at the end of the second curve.

**Answer: B.**

Figure 8 below shows a type of structure. Study it and answer questions 31 and 32.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: a type of sedimentary structure: a row of flat pebbles stacked and tilted, overlapping like roof tiles, with an arrow marking the flow direction towards the right.*

(Figure 8 is used for questions 31 and 32.)

Identify the structure illustrated above:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The flat pebbles are stacked and tilted in the same direction like roof tiles, each one overlapping the next: this is an **imbricate structure** (imbrication). Flow structure belongs to lavas, pillow and ball structures are deformation structures formed in soft sediment or underwater lava, and 'current structure' is not a specific named structure.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 8 below shows a type of structure. Study it and answer questions 31 and 32.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: a type of sedimentary structure: a row of flat pebbles stacked and tilted, overlapping like roof tiles, with an arrow marking the flow direction towards the right.*

(Figure 8 is used for questions 31 and 32.)

How was the structure in question 31 formed?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Imbrication forms when **pebbles are carried along by a current flowing in one direction**: the flat pebbles come to rest leaning against each other, dipping upstream (towards the source of the current), and so record the palaeocurrent direction. Sand moving in one direction produces cross-bedding and ripples, a current in two directions produces herringbone cross-bedding, and cooling of magma under water produces pillow lavas.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: By sand moving with current flow in one direction
By pebbles moving when current flows in one direction
By the cooling of magma under water
By the pebbles moving when current flows in two directions.

questions.enonce_markdown: A shale containing the fossils Trilobite and Graptolite was probably deposited in one of the environments below:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Graptolites were planktonic colonial animals whose remains settled in great numbers in the fine, often poorly oxygenated muds of the deeper, quiet water of the offshore basins, giving graptolitic (black) shales. A shale containing graptolites together with trilobites (Lower Palaeozoic marine animals) is therefore taken to have been deposited in a **deep marine environment** (below wave base). 'Aerobic' describes the oxygen content of the water, not a depositional environment, and the shallow options are less likely for a graptolite shale.

**Answer: C.**

Legend: Tertiary shale, Jurassic limestone, Permian sandstone, Pennsylvanian conglomerate, Mississippian coal, Precambrian gneiss. Horizontal Tertiary shale and Jurassic limestone lie above inclined Permian, Pennsylvanian, Mississippian and Precambrian beds.*

Which relative dating method can be used to date the events on the diagram?

*Options as printed:* A) Cross-cutting relationship   B) Superposition and way-up   C) Included fragments   D) Original horizontality
questions.corrige_markdown:
The diagram shows younger horizontal beds (Tertiary shale and Jurassic limestone) lying across the eroded edges of older tilted beds, and the surface between them cuts across the older layers; an inclined line running from Y across the older beds also appears to be a fault that displaces them, and a fault is younger than the beds it cuts. The relative order of the events is worked out from the law of **cross-cutting relationships** (a surface or structure that cuts across rocks is younger than the rocks it cuts), combined with superposition for the order of the beds. Because both principles are needed to order all the events and the printed options give them as alternatives, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (Cross-cutting relationship).**

What is the relationship between the horizontal and the inclined beds?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Horizontal Jurassic limestone and Tertiary shale rest on tilted older beds, so the contact between the two sets is an erosion surface that represents a long gap in the record: an **angular unconformity**. Folding and faulting describe deformation within a set of beds, and erosion is only one step in making the unconformity.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Rocks in Cameroon show different ages. Which of the following rocks are highly deformed?

*Options as printed:* A) Granite, sandstone and basalt   B) Basalt and granite   C) Schist and granite   D) Gneiss, trachyte and schist
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Cameroon the highly deformed rocks are the metamorphic rocks of the Precambrian basement (the Pan-African and older belts): **gneiss and schist**. Granite is mostly massive, although some Pan-African granites are sheared, and basalt, trachyte and the young sandstones are not strongly deformed. Option D has two strongly deformed rocks out of three (trachyte, a volcanic rock of the Cameroon Line, is not deformed) and no option has only deformed rocks, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: D (Gneiss, trachyte and schist).**

Legend: siltstone, calcareous sandstone, well cemented conglomerate, well cemented limestone, shale, sandstone; symbols for horizontal strata and dipping strata. Identify the type of unconformity on the map:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The map shows older beds, the shale with its neighbouring beds, dipping at about 31 to 39 degrees, and younger beds (conglomerate) lying across them with a dip of only about 5 degrees. When younger beds rest on older beds that dip at a **different angle**, the contact is an **angular unconformity**. A parallel unconformity (disconformity) has the same dip above and below, heterolithic is not a standard type, and a non-depositional unconformity is a simple gap in deposition.

The diagram below (Figure 12) shows a type of plate boundary. Study and answer questions 42, 43 and 44.

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

*Figure 12: a type of plate boundary (cross-section; arrow 'movement of lithospheric plates'; the dark oceanic layer bends downwards beneath the overlying plate; a volcanic feature labelled Q at the surface).*

(Figure 12 is used for questions 42, 43 and 44.)

Name the type of plate boundary represented above:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The dark oceanic layer is bent down and carried below the other plate, with a volcano above: this is a subduction zone, a **destructive boundary** (convergent margin) where lithosphere is consumed. A constructive boundary is where plates move apart and new crust forms, and a conservative (transform) boundary is where plates slide past each other without loss or gain of crust. 'Neutral boundary' is not a plate boundary type.

**Answer: B.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

The diagram below (Figure 12) shows a type of plate boundary. Study and answer questions 42, 43 and 44.

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

(Figure 12 is used for questions 42, 43 and 44.)

The composition of the feature labelled Q is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Q is the volcano above the subduction zone. There the descending slab melts and the magma rising through the overriding plate is mixed with crustal material, so the lavas are mainly **andesitic** (intermediate), typical of volcanic arcs (the Andes). Basaltic lavas belong to constructive margins and hot spots, and granitic or rhyolitic compositions are found in acid magmas.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

The diagram below (Figure 12) shows a type of plate boundary. Study and answer questions 42, 43 and 44.

![fig-12](gce-al-geology-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)

Which of the following is a characteristic of the plate boundary above?
questions.corrige_markdown:
At a subduction zone the slab descends along an inclined plane (the Benioff zone), so earthquakes occur at **shallow, intermediate and deep foci** (down to about 700 km). Symmetrical magnetic strips and high heat flow belong to constructive margins, and the formation of new crust occurs at constructive margins (a trench is a destructive feature, but 'new crust' is not).

**Answer: B.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: Two examples of ore minerals are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
An ore mineral is one from which a metal can be extracted economically. **Galena** (PbS, ore of lead) and **chalcopyrite** ($\mathrm{CuFeS_2}$, ore of copper) are both ore minerals. Fluorite and barytes (barite) are gangue or industrial minerals, iron pyrite is mined for sulphur rather than iron and corundum is an abrasive and a gem. Sphalerite (zinc) and cassiterite (tin) are ores but they are each paired with a non-ore mineral.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is gneiss commonly used as a road metal?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A road metal (aggregate for road foundations and surfacing) must resist crushing, abrasion and traffic loads. Gneiss is a hard, tough metamorphic rock with a **high compressive strength**, which is why it is quarried in many places for road stone. Being impermeable does not matter for loose aggregate, a rock that is easily quarried is also easily weathered, and binding with tar depends on a rough, clean and non-water-attracting surface more than on coarse grain size. The printed options C and D are both argued in textbooks, so the choice of D has moderate confidence.

**Answer: D.**
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection

choix.texte: It is coarse grained and binds easily with tar
It has a high compressive strength

In borehole A the water level (F-D line) stays below the surface, it is a water-table type well, and a contact spring would appear at the junction of two rocks without a borehole.

What feature is represented by F - D on the diagram?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The aquifer Y is confined between two impermeable layers and is fed at the high ground on the left. The dashed line F-D joins the levels to which the water would rise in boreholes drilled into the confined aquifer: it is the **piezometric (potentiometric) surface**. It rises above the ground near D, which is why the artesian well C flows. The water table is the top of the zone of saturation in an unconfined aquifer, and the zones of saturation and aeration are volumes of rock, not a line.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Basalts and granites usually have cracks in them as they cool. What types of springs are common in such rocks?

*Options as printed:* A) Hot springs   B) Fracture springs   C) Contact springs   D) Joint springs
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cooling igneous rocks contract and develop regular cracks called **joints** (columnar joints in basalt, sheeting and joints in granite). Water circulating in these joints comes out where they reach the surface as **joint springs**. Hot springs are heated by magma or deep circulation, and contact springs occur at the junction between a permeable and an impermeable rock. 'Fracture springs' (water issuing from faults and fractures) is a very close alternative to joint springs, so the printed options are not distinct enough to be marked automatically and the question is left open.

**Intended answer: D (Joint springs).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a rock-breaking operation commonly used in quarries in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In hard-rock quarries (granite, gneiss, basalt) the rock is broken by **blasting**: holes are drilled and loaded with explosives. Stripping is the removal of the overburden before quarrying, scraping is a surface operation for soft material and slumping is a natural mass movement, not a quarrying operation.

**Answer: C.**
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection
